lessons.title: The resources an abattoir uses
lessons.html:
What resource optimisation means

Optimising resources means getting the most useful output from the people, animals, water, energy, materials and equipment the abattoir uses, without compromising food safety, welfare, safety or legal compliance. The foreman oversees this across the shift and looks for waste.

Main resources and their waste

ResourceTypical waste
Livestock and carcassBruising, over-trimming, contamination trims, avoidable condemnations, poor yield in deboning
By-productsDamaged hides, offal contaminated or not saved, blood and fat lost to drains
LabourWaiting time, poor station balance, unnecessary overtime, absenteeism
WaterHoses left running, leaks, washing with more water than needed
ElectricityChiller doors left open, equipment running when not needed, poor insulation
ChemicalsOver-strength mixing, spills, using the wrong product
ConsumablesLost knives and protective clothing, wasted bags and labels
EquipmentBreakdowns from poor maintenance, misuse

Measure first

You cannot manage what you do not measure. Use figures per animal or per tonne of carcass, such as litres of water per head, kWh per head, labour hours per head, and trim mass per carcass. Compare shifts, weeks and seasons to find where waste is growing.

lessons.title: Optimising labour, yield and by-products
lessons.html:
Labour

  • Balance the line: time each station and match staff to the work. Move people from stations with idle time to bottlenecks.
  • Multi-skill workers so absence does not stop the line or force expensive overtime.
  • Plan the day: start on time with everything ready; avoid waiting for animals or equipment.
  • Control overtime: approve it in advance and check it against the reason.

Yield

Every kilogram of meat lost through bruising, contamination or careless trimming is income lost.

  • Work with procurement and the lairage team to reduce bruising: good loading ramps, no sticks, calm handling.
  • Train dressers in hygienic technique so fewer contamination trims are needed.
  • Set trimming standards: trim enough to remove the defect, no more.
  • Monitor carcass mass loss in chillers (shrink) and keep chiller conditions correct.
  • In deboning, follow cutting specifications and track saleable yield per carcass.

Example

An abattoir slaughters 250 cattle a day. Trim records show an average of 2.2 kg trimmed per carcass for contamination and bruising. After retraining and better lairage handling, this drops to 1.4 kg. At R60 per kg the saving is 0.8 x 250 x R60 = R12 000 per day.

By-products

  • Hides and skins: careful flaying without knife cuts; correct salting or fast delivery to the tannery.
  • Offal: hygienic handling so it passes inspection; quick chilling.
  • Blood and fat: collect rather than wash into the drain; this also reduces effluent load and costs.

lessons.title: Water, energy and materials
lessons.html:
Water

Abattoirs use a lot of water, and South Africa is a water-scarce country. Water use and effluent are controlled under the National Water Act 36 of 1998 and municipal by-laws.

  • Fix leaks quickly and report dripping taps and broken hoses.
  • Fit hoses with trigger nozzles that stop when released.
  • Dry clean (scrape and collect solids) before wet cleaning.
  • Use water at the right pressure and temperature for each task.
  • Never reduce water used for hygiene below what the procedures require.

Energy

  • Keep chiller doors closed and seals in good condition.
  • Do not overload chillers; plan the kill to match capacity.
  • Switch off lights and equipment in areas not in use, where safe to do so.
  • Maintain refrigeration and boilers so they run efficiently.
  • Plan high-energy activities with load shedding and tariff times in mind where possible.

Materials and consumables

  • Issue protective clothing, knives and chemicals through a register.
  • Mix chemicals to label strength using measuring equipment, not guesswork.
  • Store materials correctly so they are not damaged.
  • Count and reconcile stock monthly.

Involving the team

Workers see waste every day. Ask for their ideas, share the savings figures, and recognise improvements. Make resource use part of the start-of-shift meeting from time to time.

Key points

  • Optimise resources without compromising food safety, welfare, safety or the law.
  • Measure use per animal to find and track waste.
  • Balance the line and multi-skill workers to use labour well.
  • Reduce bruising and over-trimming to protect yield.
  • Save water and energy through leak repair, dry cleaning and closed chiller doors.
